prompt: Cinematic film still, anamorphic 35mm wide: a camp kitchen gutted down to bare timber studs, plywood patches and a water-stained ceiling overhead. On a painted-wood workbench at the right third, a fat ribbon-bound stack of blank court papers — the award — beside one thin lone envelope, tiny against the stack. A single work lamp rakes warm ochre light across the bone-white paper from the left rear; the unfinished room falls into charcoal and deep pine green dusk through a bare window opening. rationale: The story turns on one decisive place — the camp rebuilt down to the studs that still lets water in — and one decisive gap: the order versus the money. Cinematic_still lets the gutted room carry the builder's failure while the thick judgment stack against the lone envelope states the verdict-versus-cash conflict in a single glance, with dusk atmosphere no macro or collage could ground.
cue: The order was real. The money was not.
subject: a thick ribbon-bound stack of court papers beside one thin envelope on a plywood bench
core_thesis: A court order is not money in your hand: a Maine homeowner's very real $630,500 judgment trickles out at an agreed $125 a week — 97 years of checks — because the builder behind it was unregistered, unregulated and effectively judgment-proof.
core_conflict: The paper victory versus the collectible cash — a legally airtight award collides with an unlicensed, assetless builder the state itself admits it often cannot collect from, so the homeowner's only real leverage was the money never paid in the first place.
composition: Extreme asymmetric wide framing: the judgment stack and single envelope sit on the right third of a makeshift bench, while bare timber stud framing recedes into dusk shadow across the generous left negative space.
